edges.description: Leg edema and impaired lymphatic drainage act as an independent local susceptibility factor that favors dermal infection after a barrier break admits streptococci.
A compromised skin barrier enables beta-hemolytic streptococci to enter and establish infection in superficial dermis and dermal lymphatics.
Streptococcal infection in superficial dermis and dermal lymphatics produces the sharply demarcated inflammatory erythema and early constitutional symptoms of acute erysipelas.
Erysipelas episodes can worsen lymphatic drainage and feed a recurrence-prone edema-infection cycle.
Upper-dermal inflammation produces the bright red, shiny erythema used to diagnose erysipelas clinically.
Systemic inflammatory signaling during acute erysipelas commonly manifests with fever among the early constitutional symptoms.
The same early constitutional inflammatory response can present with chills or shivers around erythema onset.
Local dermal inflammation can make the erythematous lesion painful or tender in acute erysipelas.
Repeated erysipelas episodes increase the prevalence of subclinical lymphedema, feeding the lymphatic susceptibility that permits subsequent episodes.
Erysipelas-associated lymphatic damage can persist as chronic lymphedema and, in severe cases, elephantiasis.
Erysipelas involving superficial dermal lymphatics can be complicated by clinically recognized lymphangitis.
Mechanical or inflammatory barrier defects increase susceptibility to streptococcal dermal entry.
Interdigital fungal disease and maceration open cutaneous entry sites for beta-hemolytic streptococci.
Edematous and lymphatically impaired tissue has diminished local fluid clearance and is prone to recurrent streptococcal infection.

nodes.description: The acute host response to streptococcal growth in the superficial dermis produces bright, well-demarcated erythema and early systemic symptoms such as fever and chills.
Chills or shivers can occur early in acute erysipelas before or alongside the visible erythematous lesion.

nodes.description: Traumatic wounds, toe-web intertrigo, excoriated dermatoses, and plantar scaling lesions breach the skin and create portals through which streptococci can reach the superficial dermis.

evidence.reference_title: Risk factors for erysipelas of the leg in Tunisia: a multicenter case-control study.
evidence.snippet: disruption of the cutaneous barrier (i.e. traumatic wound, toe-web intertrigo, excoriated leg dermatosis or plantar squamous lesions) and leg edema were independently associated with erysipelas of the leg, with respective odds ratios of 13.6 (95% confidence interval: 6.0-31) and 7.0 (1.3-38).

evidence.snippet: During the prophylaxis phase, 30 of 136 participants in the penicillin group (22%) had a recurrence, as compared with 51 of 138 participants in the placebo group (37%) (hazard ratio, 0.55; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.35 to 0.86; P=0.01), yielding a number needed to treat to prevent one recurrent cellulitis episode of 5 (95% CI, 4 to 9).
